divide.name: Open and closed sets
divide.brief: This part covers the basic set structure of the real line: epsilon-neighbourhoods, open sets defined through interior points, limit (accumulation) points and isolated points, closed sets defined as sets containing all their limit points, and the sequence characterisations (x is a limit point of A exactly when some sequence in A minus {x} converges to x; A is closed exactly when every convergent sequence in A has its limit in A). Also closure (A together with its limit points, the smallest closed set containing A, with the closure of Q being R as the density example) and interior (the largest open subset), the duality that a set is open exactly when its complement is closed, and unions and intersections: arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets are open, with (-1/n, 1/n) showing an infinite intersection can fail, and the matching statements for closed sets via De Morgan's laws. Standard examples: open and closed intervals, [a,b) as neither, Z, {1/n} and Q. Edges: compactness belongs to 'Compact sets' and connectedness, perfect sets and the Cantor set to 'Connected sets, perfect sets and the Cantor set'. Convergence of sequences comes from 'Sequences', density of the rationals from 'The real numbers', and indexed unions and De Morgan's laws from 'Logic, sets and proof'; they are used, not retaught. Continuous functions are not studied here. What matters for this learner: being able to prove from the definitions that a given set is or is not open or closed, and to switch fluently between the neighbourhood view and the sequence view, because later parts use both.

divide.name: Compact sets
divide.brief: This part covers compactness on the real line: sequential compactness (every sequence in K has a subsequence converging to a point of K), the proof via Bolzano-Weierstrass that a set is sequentially compact exactly when it is closed and bounded, open covers and finite subcovers, the open-cover definition of compactness, and the Heine-Borel theorem with full proof that the three conditions (closed and bounded, sequentially compact, every open cover has a finite subcover) are equivalent (for example by repeated bisection and the nested interval property). It also covers the nested compact set property (a decreasing sequence of nonempty compact sets has nonempty intersection) and explicit reasons why (0,1) and R are not compact, both with a sequence that has no convergent subsequence in the set and with an open cover that has no finite subcover ((1/n, 1) and (-n, n)). Edges: open sets, closed sets, limit points and closure come from 'Open and closed sets'. Bolzano-Weierstrass and subsequences come from 'Sequences' and the nested interval property from 'The real numbers'; they are used, not reproved. Continuous images of compact sets, the extreme value theorem and uniform continuity belong to 'Limits of functions and continuity'. Perfect sets and the Cantor set belong to 'Connected sets, perfect sets and the Cantor set', which uses the nested compact set property from here. What matters for this learner: compactness is the hypothesis that turns local information (something true near each point) into global information (true on the whole set) through a finite subcover, and the learner should be able to say in their own words, and prove, why (0,1) and R are not compact while [a,b] is. Keep it aimed at what continuity and integration need.

divide.name: Connected sets, perfect sets and the Cantor set
divide.brief: This part covers separated sets and connected sets (a set is disconnected when it is the union of two nonempty separated sets), examples such as Q and the union of two disjoint intervals being disconnected, and the theorem with proof that the connected subsets of the real line are exactly the intervals (using the supremum). Then perfect sets (closed with no isolated points), the theorem that a nonempty perfect set is uncountable (proved with nested compact sets), and the Cantor set as the key example: its construction by removing middle thirds, that it is closed and compact, that the removed lengths sum to 1, that it is uncountable (via ternary expansions or the perfect set theorem), perfect, and contains no interval (totally disconnected). The part ends with a short note that all the ideas of this topic (neighbourhoods, open and closed sets, compactness, connectedness) use only the distance |x - y| and so generalise to metric spaces, where closed and bounded no longer implies compact. Edges: open and closed sets, closure and isolated points come from 'Open and closed sets'; compactness and the nested compact set property come from 'Compact sets'. Supremum and uncountability come from 'The real numbers', geometric series from 'Series of real numbers'. The intermediate value theorem itself belongs to 'Limits of functions and continuity', which uses the intervals theorem from here. Metric spaces are only mentioned; they are developed in 'Where analysis leads'. What matters for this learner: that connectedness is the reason behind the intermediate value theorem, so they should understand the proof that connected means interval, and that the Cantor set is the standard counterexample that tests intuitions about size (uncountable, yet containing no interval and of total length zero). Keep it short.
